Predators of those rodents, such as owls and martens, respond in turn, and ticks and the diseases they carry may also fluctuate with the abundance of hosts. Deer, wild boar, and bears feed heavily on mast, and their condition and reproduction can reflect its availability. Seedling establishment is typically concentrated in the years following a good crop, so the age structure of many forests records past mast events.

Regeneration and Gap Dynamics

Temperate deciduous forests renew themselves through a continuing sequence of small and large disturbances. Although a mature stand may appear stable, its structure is constantly being rearranged as trees die, lose limbs, or are uprooted. The openings created in the canopy, known as gaps, are the main setting in which many woodland trees begin their growth to maturity, and the study of how gaps form and fill is central to understanding forest composition over long periods.

Formation of Gaps

Gaps arise from several causes. Wind is the most widespread, snapping trunks or toppling trees whose roots have been weakened by saturated soil, decay, or shallow rooting. Fungal pathogens, including root and butt rots, often predispose large trees to such failure. Ice storms, drought, insect defoliation, and introduced diseases such as chestnut blight and Dutch elm disease also remove canopy individuals. Where a single tree falls, the gap is small, but a storm may bring down many trees together and produce a much larger opening. Fire, once a significant factor in some regions, and clearance by people have also shaped the pattern of openings in many landscapes.

A fallen tree leaves a characteristic microtopography. The upturned root plate exposes mineral soil, and the hollow it leaves behind, together with the mound formed where the root plate settles, creates a patchwork of wet and dry, nutrient-rich and nutrient-poor surfaces. These pits and mounds persist for decades and provide seedbeds for species that need bare soil, such as birches, while the decaying trunk offers a different substrate for mosses, fungi, and some tree seedlings.

Light, Soil, and Seedlings

The canopy of a closed deciduous forest intercepts most incoming light, and the understory in summer is deeply shaded. In spring, before leaves expand, much more light reaches the ground, and spring ephemeral herbs take advantage of this brief interval. Beneath the full canopy, seedlings of shade-tolerant trees such as beech and sugar maple can persist for many years in a suppressed condition, growing slowly and forming what is often called a seedling or sapling bank. When a gap opens above them, these advance regeneration individuals may respond quickly with accelerated growth.

Gaps also change conditions below ground. Removal of a large tree reduces water uptake, so soil moisture often rises, and increased warmth and light speed the decomposition of litter, temporarily raising the availability of nitrogen and other nutrients. Mycorrhizal networks are disrupted when the host tree dies, and seedlings that are linked to different fungal partners may establish with varying success. Seed predation by rodents, browsing by deer, and competition from ferns or brambles can strongly influence which seedlings survive.

Species Strategies

Tree species differ in how they exploit gaps. Shade-intolerant, or pioneer, species such as aspen, birch, and tulip tree produce abundant, readily dispersed seed and grow rapidly in full light, but they are poorly suited to persist beneath a closed canopy. Intermediate species, including many oaks and ashes, require moderate light and may be favoured by larger openings. Strongly shade-tolerant species, such as beech, hemlock, and sugar maple, can recruit in very small gaps or beneath intact canopy. The size, frequency, and timing of gaps therefore help determine which species are represented in the next generation.

Oak regeneration has attracted particular attention. Oaks are long-lived and produce large acorns that are heavily consumed by animals, and their seedlings often struggle in deep shade. In many regions, where fire and other disturbances have declined, shade-tolerant competitors have increasingly replaced oaks in the understory.

Gap Phase Replacement

The idea of gap-phase replacement describes the forest as a mosaic of patches at different stages of recovery. Each patch moves through colonisation, rapid growth, thinning, and eventual canopy closure, until another disturbance restarts the process. Over a wide area, this produces a varied age structure and supports diverse communities, including cavity-nesting birds that use dead and dying trees, insects that feed on decaying wood, and shrub-layer species favoured by increased light. Where very old stands survive, the legacy of past gaps remains visible in the arrangement of trees, fallen logs, and uneven ground.

Succession from Field to Forest

When farmland in a temperate region is abandoned, it does not remain open for long. Left alone, a cultivated field or pasture gradually returns to woodland through a sequence of changes known as secondary succession. Unlike primary succession, which begins on bare rock or fresh volcanic or glacial deposits, secondary succession starts on land that already has soil, a store of buried seeds, and often the living roots of earlier plants. For this reason it proceeds more quickly, and much of the deciduous forest of eastern North America, western Europe and eastern Asia has arisen in this way on land once cleared for agriculture.

The Annual and Herbaceous Phase

The first season or two after abandonment is typically dominated by annual weeds, which germinate from the seed bank in the disturbed soil. Ragweed, crabgrass and other fast-growing, short-lived species flower and set seed quickly. They are soon joined and then replaced by perennial grasses and herbs such as goldenrod, asters, broomsedge and Queen Anne's lace. In Europe, comparable communities include thistles, docks, bramble and tall grasses. Insects, seed-eating birds and small mammals such as voles use this open habitat, and birds including sparrows, meadowlarks and bobolinks nest in the dense grass where the ground is undisturbed.

Shrubs and Pioneer Trees

Woody plants begin to establish within a few years. Seeds arrive by wind, water and animals; birds in particular deposit berries and fruit beneath fence lines and perches, creating islands of shrubs such as sumac, hawthorn, blackberry, dogwood and eastern red cedar. Pioneer trees follow. These are light-demanding species with abundant, widely dispersed seed and rapid early growth, including birch, aspen, poplar, pin cherry, sassafras and various pines. Their canopy closes over the herbs, which are shaded out, and the field becomes a young, dense thicket. Birds of shrubland and thicket, such as chats, towhees and some warblers, replace those of open grassland.

Pioneer trees are generally short-lived and intolerant of shade. Their own seedlings cannot grow well beneath their canopy, which means they prepare the site for other species rather than perpetuating themselves. Leaf litter accumulates, organic matter builds in the topsoil, and the soil becomes cooler, moister and more sheltered from wind.

Arrival of the Shade-Tolerant Trees

Beneath the pioneers, seedlings of slower-growing, shade-tolerant species establish. Oaks, hickories, ashes, maples, beech and, in Europe, species such as hornbeam and lime may appear, depending on region and seed source. Heavy-seeded trees such as oak and hickory depend largely on animals, especially jays and squirrels, which carry and bury acorns and nuts, sometimes far from the parent tree. As the pioneers age and die, gaps open and the understory trees grow up to take their place. Over many decades, the canopy comes to be dominated by the long-lived species typical of mature forest.

Changes Below Ground

Succession is as visible in the soil as in the vegetation. Fungi respond to the changing plant community. Grassland and early shrubland soils tend to be associated with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, whereas many forest trees, notably oaks, beeches and birches, form ectomycorrhizal partnerships, and the fungal community shifts accordingly. Decomposer fungi multiply as woody debris and leaf litter increase, and a distinct organic horizon forms on top of the mineral soil. Earthworm and microbial activity, soil structure and acidity all change, often over a longer period than the change in tree cover.

A Process, Not a Fixed Path

The sequence described here is a general pattern, and its details vary with climate, soil, the surrounding seed sources, past land use and browsing by deer or livestock. Fire, storms, disease and renewed clearing can interrupt or redirect the process. Ecologists no longer regard the end point as a single, permanent climax community. Instead, a mature forest is seen as a shifting mosaic, continually altered by disturbance and regrowth. Even so, old stone walls running through the middle of mature woods, and the occasional wide-limbed tree that grew in open pasture, remain visible evidence of the fields from which many of these forests came.

Soil Formation and Profiles

The soils of temperate deciduous forests develop through the long interaction of parent material, climate, topography, living organisms and time. Because these forests occupy regions with moderate rainfall, a distinct cold season and a warm growing season, the processes that shape their soils differ from those of boreal conifer forests to the north and grasslands in drier continental interiors. Much of the soil beneath present-day deciduous woodland in North America, Europe and eastern Asia began forming after the retreat of the last glaciers, so that many profiles are geologically young and reflect the glacial deposits, loess, river alluvium or weathered bedrock on which they rest.

Parent Material and Climate

Parent material determines the initial mineral composition, texture and nutrient supply of a soil. Limestone and other calcareous rocks yield base-rich soils with a near-neutral reaction, while sandstones and granites tend to produce more acidic, coarser-textured soils. Glacial till, which mixes fragments of many rock types, often gives loamy soils of moderate fertility. Climate acts mainly through temperature and water movement. Rain and snowmelt percolate downward through the soil, carrying dissolved substances and fine particles with them. Winter cold slows biological activity, whereas the warm months allow rapid decomposition and root growth.

The Role of Leaf Litter and Organisms

Deciduous trees shed their leaves each autumn, delivering a large annual input of organic matter to the ground. The quality of this litter strongly influences soil development. Leaves of species such as ash, linden, elm and maple decompose quickly and are rich in calcium, favouring mild humus and abundant earthworms. Oak and beech leaves are tougher and more acidic, and they break down more slowly, which can lead to a thicker accumulation of partly decayed material on the surface.

Decomposition is carried out by a succession of organisms. Bacteria and fungi break down cellulose and, in the case of many fungi, lignin. Springtails, mites, millipedes, woodlice and earthworms fragment the litter and mix it into the mineral soil. Where earthworms are active, the organic and mineral layers are blended thoroughly, producing a crumbly, dark upper horizon. Where they are scarce, litter accumulates in distinct layers. Mycorrhizal fungi, which form partnerships with tree roots, also contribute by moving nutrients and by binding soil particles together.

Characteristic Soil Types

Many temperate deciduous forests are associated with soils classed as Alfisols in the United States system and as Luvisols in the international World Reference Base. These soils show a moderate degree of leaching, in which clay is gradually carried from the upper layers and deposited deeper in the profile. Where drainage is good and the parent material is rich in bases, brown forest soils, also called Cambisols or Inceptisols, are common; these show weaker horizon differentiation. In cooler or more acidic settings, especially beneath oak, beech or mixed stands with conifers, podzolisation may occur. In this process organic acids move iron and aluminium downward, leaving a pale, bleached layer beneath the surface. Poorly drained hollows may develop gleyed soils with grey and rust-coloured mottling caused by waterlogging.

Typical Profile

A mature forest soil is arranged in horizons, or layers, that can be seen in a cut face.

The O horizon at the top consists of organic material. Its upper part contains recognisable fallen leaves and twigs, and its lower part holds fragmented and humified matter.

The A horizon is a dark mineral layer enriched with decomposed organic matter and heavily penetrated by roots and soil animals.

The E horizon, present in some soils, is a paler layer from which clay, iron or organic compounds have been removed.

The B horizon accumulates clay, iron oxides or other materials washed down from above and is often more compact and more strongly coloured.

The C horizon is weathered parent material showing little biological alteration, and it grades into unweathered bedrock or sediment below.

Soil Disturbance and Variation

Profiles are not static. Falling trees uproot soil and create pit-and-mound microtopography that mixes horizons and creates varied habitats for seedlings, fungi and invertebrates. Burrowing mammals, fire, past agriculture and human land use leave lasting marks. Former plough layers can persist as sharply defined boundaries beneath regrown woodland, and compaction from grazing or machinery can affect drainage and root growth for many decades.

Leaf Litter and Decomposition

Each autumn, the canopy of a temperate deciduous forest releases a large pulse of organic material to the ground. Leaves, together with twigs, bud scales, flowers, fruits and occasional fallen branches, accumulate as a layer of litter that covers the mineral soil. This layer is both a habitat and a resource store, and its gradual breakdown links the trees above with the soils, fungi and invertebrates below. Before leaves fall, trees withdraw many of their mobile nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, and the green pigment chlorophyll is broken down. This is why autumn leaves reveal yellow and orange pigments and why fallen leaves are relatively poor in nutrients compared with living foliage.

Variation Among Species

Leaf litter is not uniform. Species differ in the toughness of their leaves, in the concentration of lignin and tannins, and in the amount of calcium and other minerals they contain. Leaves of ash, elm, lime and maple tend to break down quickly, often within a single year, because they are soft and comparatively rich in nutrients. Oak and beech leaves are tougher and more resistant, and they may persist as recognisable leaves for much longer. Chemical defences that protect living leaves from herbivores, including phenolic compounds, continue to affect the litter after leaf fall, slowing colonisation by decomposers. In mixed woods, the blending of fast and slow litter types produces a patchwork of conditions that supports a wider range of organisms than a stand of a single species.

Stages of Breakdown

Decomposition proceeds through overlapping processes. Soon after leaf fall, rain leaches soluble sugars, phenolics and some minerals from the leaves into the soil. Bacteria and microscopic fungi, many of which already live on leaf surfaces, begin to colonise the tissue. Larger fungi, including many species of the genera Mycena and Marasmius, then extend threads of hyphae through the litter and produce enzymes capable of digesting cellulose. Some fungi, including white-rot species, are able to attack lignin, which few other organisms can degrade. The pale, bleached appearance of heavily decayed leaves often reflects this activity.

The Role of Soil Animals

Invertebrates accelerate the process by fragmenting litter and mixing it with soil. Earthworms pull leaves into their burrows, where the material is partly digested and combined with mineral particles. Millipedes, woodlice, springtails, mites, snails and the larvae of many flies feed on partly decayed leaves, and much of their effect comes from the increased surface area their feeding creates for microbes. Many of these animals prefer leaves that have already been softened by fungi, so microbial and animal activity are closely connected. Predators such as centipedes, beetles, spiders and salamanders feed on the decomposers, forming a food web that operates largely out of sight within the litter.

Humus and Soil Formation

Material that resists rapid breakdown becomes humus, a dark, stable organic matter that binds mineral particles into crumbs, retains water and holds nutrients in forms available to roots. Forests on base-rich soils with abundant earthworms typically develop a mild humus, called mull, in which litter is quickly incorporated and the boundary between organic and mineral layers is blurred. On acidic, nutrient-poor soils, where earthworms are scarce and fungi dominate, litter accumulates in distinct layers, producing a thicker form known as mor. Intermediate conditions yield a form called moder. These humus types are used by soil scientists as indicators of forest fertility and biological activity.

Ecological Importance

Litter shapes the forest in other ways. It insulates the soil, moderates moisture and temperature, and suppresses or favours the germination of seedlings depending on its depth and chemistry. Spring wildflowers often complete much of their growth before the canopy closes, taking advantage of nutrients released from the previous year's leaves. Ground-nesting birds, small mammals, reptiles and amphibians use the layer for cover and foraging. Fires, droughts, changes in earthworm populations and warming climates can all alter the rate at which litter decays, with consequences for nutrient cycling and for the amount of carbon held in forest soils.

Nutrient Cycling

Temperate deciduous forests retain and recirculate most of the nutrients that pass through them. Because the trees are long-lived and the soils beneath them are often old and leached, the forest depends less on fresh supplies from rock weathering or rainfall than on the steady reuse of material already held in living tissue, leaf litter and humus. The seasonal rhythm of leaf growth and leaf fall sets the tempo of this cycle.

Uptake and Storage

During the growing season, roots draw nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and other elements from the soil solution and transport them to the crown. Much of this uptake is mediated by fungi. Ectomycorrhizal species, which are especially associated with oaks, beeches, birches and hornbeams, form sheaths around fine root tips and extend threads of mycelium into the soil. These threads reach pockets of organic matter that roots alone could not exploit, and they return nitrogen and phosphorus to the tree in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis. Maples and ashes, by contrast, usually host arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, which are particularly effective at gathering phosphorus. The balance between these two fungal groups in a stand influences how quickly nutrients circulate.

Resorption Before Leaf Fall

In autumn, as chlorophyll breaks down and the green pigment fades, the tree withdraws a substantial part of the nitrogen and phosphorus from its leaves and stores it in twigs, branches, trunk and roots. This resorption conserves scarce elements and allows the tree to build new leaves the following spring from internal reserves. Elements such as calcium, which are not readily moved within the plant, remain in the leaf and reach the ground in the litter. The yellow and orange tones of many autumn leaves are carotenoid pigments that were present all along and become visible as the green fades.

Litterfall and Decomposition

The falling leaves form a layer on the forest floor that is, in effect, an annual delivery of organic matter and minerals. Decomposition of this material is carried out by a succession of organisms. Bacteria and fungi begin the chemical breakdown, while earthworms, springtails, mites, millipedes, woodlice and fly larvae fragment the litter, mix it with mineral soil and expose fresh surfaces for microbial attack. Leaves differ in how readily they decay. Those of ash, elm, lime and maple, which are rich in nutrients and low in tannins, are consumed relatively quickly, whereas oak and beech leaves, with tougher tissue and more resistant compounds, persist longer and may build a deeper litter layer.

Fallen branches and trunks supply a slower stream of nutrients. Wood-decaying fungi, including white-rot and brown-rot species, break down cellulose and lignin over many years, and in doing so release nutrients and create habitat for beetles, mosses and other organisms. Dead wood also stores carbon and water and acts as a long-term reservoir within the forest.

Humus and Soil Processes

Partly decomposed material accumulates as humus, which holds water and binds nutrient ions that might otherwise wash away. In mild, well-drained sites with abundant earthworms, a mull humus forms, in which organic matter is thoroughly mixed with mineral soil and nutrients circulate rapidly. In cooler or more acidic sites, a mor humus may develop, with a distinct layer of poorly decomposed litter and slower release of nitrogen. Soil microbes convert organic nitrogen to ammonium and then to nitrate, a process that varies with temperature, moisture and acidity.

Inputs and Losses

Small gains arrive through rainfall, dust, the weathering of minerals and nitrogen fixation by certain bacteria. Losses occur through leaching into streams and groundwater, gaseous emissions, fire and the removal of timber. Spring is a vulnerable period, because soil nutrients can be washed away before leaves emerge, and the early-flowering herbs of the forest floor, such as wood anemone and bluebell, are thought to help hold these nutrients in living tissue until the canopy closes. Their leaves then die back and return the nutrients to the soil, adding another small loop to the cycle.

Soil Microbes and Invertebrates

Beneath the leaf litter of a temperate deciduous forest lies a community of organisms that is far more diverse than the trees and animals visible above it. Bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, nematodes, mites, springtails, earthworms, and the larvae of many insects together carry out most of the decomposition and nutrient cycling on which the forest depends. Their activity converts the annual fall of leaves, twigs, and dead roots into forms of nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements that trees can absorb.

Microbial Decomposers

Bacteria are the most numerous soil organisms, and they occupy nearly every microhabitat, from the surface of fresh litter to the films of water around mineral grains. Many are specialised in particular tasks. Some break down simple sugars released from fresh leaves, while others attack more resistant compounds. Actinobacteria, which are common in forest soils, are known for degrading tough plant polymers and for producing the compounds that give disturbed soil its characteristic earthy smell. Other groups transform nitrogen: some fix atmospheric nitrogen, others convert ammonium to nitrate, and others return nitrogen to the atmosphere under waterlogged conditions.

Fungi dominate the decomposition of woody and leaf material in most deciduous woodlands. Their threadlike hyphae penetrate litter and dead wood, secreting enzymes that dismantle cellulose and lignin. Saprotrophic species, including many basidiomycetes, are particularly important in the later stages of leaf decay. Beneath the surface, mycorrhizal fungi form partnerships with tree roots. Oaks, beeches, birches, and hornbeams generally associate with ectomycorrhizal fungi, whereas maples and ashes more often host arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. In both cases the fungus extends the effective reach of the root system and receives sugars from the tree in exchange for water and nutrients.

Soil Fauna

Invertebrates fragment and mix the organic material that microbes then colonise. Researchers often group them by body size. The smallest, such as protists and nematodes, live in the water films between soil particles. Many protists and some nematodes graze on bacteria, and their feeding releases nutrients that would otherwise remain locked in microbial cells. Other nematodes feed on fungi, on roots, or on other nematodes.

Mites and springtails make up much of the middle size range. Oribatid mites feed on decaying plant matter and fungi, and they are slow-growing and long-lived relative to many other soil animals. Springtails graze fungal hyphae and spores and are often abundant in the upper litter layer. Their droppings add to the structure of the humus.

The largest animals include earthworms, millipedes, woodlice, beetle larvae, and fly larvae. Millipedes and woodlice shred fallen leaves, increasing the surface area available to microbes. Earthworms have a still greater effect on soil structure. Species that feed at the surface pull leaves into burrows, and deep-burrowing species move material between layers, mixing organic matter with mineral soil. Their tunnels improve drainage and aeration, and their casts form stable aggregates. In parts of North America that were glaciated, earthworms are largely non-native, and their arrival has been linked to the loss of the thick organic layer that formerly covered the forest floor, with consequences for understory plants and salamanders.

Seasonal and Ecological Patterns

Soil life follows the seasons. Autumn leaf fall supplies a large pulse of fresh material, and microbial activity rises while soils remain mild and moist. Cold winters slow decomposition without halting it entirely, and some microbes remain active beneath snow. Spring brings renewed root growth and a flush of nutrient uptake by trees and wildflowers. Summer drought can restrict activity, particularly in the upper litter.

The soil community is also linked to other parts of the forest. Fungal networks connect trees, invertebrates feed birds and small mammals, and the rate of decomposition influences which plants can thrive. Because these organisms are small and hidden, they were long overlooked, but advances in molecular methods since the late twentieth century have revealed how many species remain undescribed.

Mycorrhizal Networks

Beneath the floor of a temperate deciduous forest, most tree roots are intimately associated with fungi. This partnership, known as mycorrhiza (from the Greek for "fungus root"), is among the most widespread and ecologically significant relationships in terrestrial ecosystems. The fungus colonises the fine roots of a tree and extends a web of microscopic filaments, called hyphae, into the surrounding soil. In exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis, the fungus supplies the plant with water and mineral nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, which it absorbs far more effectively than roots alone can.

Types of Mycorrhiza

Two main forms dominate in temperate deciduous woodland. Ectomycorrhizal fungi form a sheath, or mantle, around the outside of root tips and grow between the root's cortical cells without penetrating them, creating a structure called the Hartig net. This type is characteristic of oaks, beeches, birches, hornbeams, limes and willows. Many of the familiar fruiting bodies of the forest floor belong to ectomycorrhizal species, including chanterelles, boletes, milk-caps, russulas and amanitas. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, by contrast, penetrate the cells of the root and form finely branched structures within them. They are associated with maples, ashes, and many shrubs and herbaceous plants of the woodland understorey. These fungi produce few conspicuous mushrooms and are generally identified by their spores and genetic markers.

Some forests contain a mixture of both types, and the balance between them influences how nutrients cycle through the soil. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can access organic nitrogen held in decaying leaf litter, whereas arbuscular fungi depend more heavily on nutrients already released in mineral form. Stands dominated by one type or the other can therefore differ in the thickness of their litter layer and the speed at which it decomposes.

The "Wood Wide Web"

Because a single fungus may colonise the roots of several trees at once, individuals can become linked through shared hyphae. Such connections are often described as common mycorrhizal networks, and the popular press has called them the "wood wide web". Experiments beginning in the late 1990s, using radioactive and stable isotopes of carbon, showed that carbon could move between neighbouring trees of different species through soil fungi. Later work reported movement of nitrogen, phosphorus, water and signalling compounds as well.

The ecological meaning of these exchanges remains debated. Some researchers have proposed that large, established trees support seedlings in the shade through the network, and that trees may share resources with injured neighbours. Others point out that much of the evidence comes from greenhouse or laboratory studies, that carbon transfer may be small compared with what a seedling obtains from its own leaves, and that it is difficult to show that transfer benefits the plants rather than simply occurring as a by-product of fungal growth. Seedlings establishing within an existing network may nonetheless gain faster access to compatible fungi, which can improve early survival. Current scholarship generally treats networks as real and widespread, while regarding claims about cooperation or "communication" between trees with caution.

Other Roles

Mycorrhizal fungi also affect soil structure. Hyphae bind mineral particles and organic matter into aggregates, improving aeration and water retention. Some fungal products, such as the protein glomalin produced by arbuscular species, contribute to long-term soil carbon storage. Fungal tissue itself serves as food for soil animals including springtails, mites and nematodes, and for larger consumers such as squirrels, deer and wild boar, which eat and disperse fruiting bodies and their spores.

Certain plants exploit the network without contributing to it. Mycoheterotrophic species, such as the pale, chlorophyll-lacking yellow bird's-nest, obtain carbon from fungi that are themselves attached to green trees. Many woodland orchids depend on fungi during germination, when their tiny seeds contain almost no reserves.

Vulnerabilities

Mycorrhizal communities are sensitive to disturbance. Clear-felling, soil compaction, ploughing and prolonged nitrogen deposition from air pollution can reduce fungal diversity and alter which species persist. Because the fungi live out of sight, they have historically received less attention in conservation planning than the trees they support, though recognition of their importance in woodland management has grown in recent decades.

Wood-Decay Fungi

Wood-decay fungi are the principal agents by which the bulk of a temperate deciduous forest's woody biomass is returned to the soil. Standing trees, fallen limbs, trunks and buried roots are composed largely of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, compounds that resist breakdown by most organisms. Only a limited group of fungi, together with some bacteria acting more slowly, can dismantle them. Their activity shapes nutrient cycling, creates habitat for many other species, and influences the structure of the forest itself.

Modes of decay

Wood-decay fungi are traditionally grouped by the kind of damage they cause. White-rot fungi, most of them basidiomycetes, produce enzymes that degrade lignin as well as cellulose and hemicellulose. The wood they attack becomes pale, fibrous or stringy, and in some cases is bleached in patches. Brown-rot fungi remove the cellulose and hemicellulose while leaving the lignin largely modified but intact. The residue is brown, brittle and breaks into cubical blocks, and it eventually becomes a crumbly material that contributes to the humus layer. Soft-rot fungi, mostly ascomycetes, tend to work in wood that is very wet or otherwise unfavourable to basidiomycetes, and they produce cavities within the cell walls.

In broadleaved forests white rot is the more common type, whereas brown rot is more strongly associated with conifers. Even so, brown-rotting species occur on oaks, chestnuts and other hardwoods, and they can be conspicuous where they do.

Parasites, heart-rotters and saprotrophs

Fungi differ in the condition of the wood they colonise. Some are weak parasites or opportunists that enter living trees through wounds, broken branches or damaged roots. Heart-rot fungi grow in the dead central wood of a living tree, often for decades, hollowing the trunk while the outer sapwood continues to carry water. The beefsteak fungus, Fistulina hepatica, on oak, and the sulphur polypore, Laetiporus sulphureus, are well-known examples. Honey fungus, Armillaria, spreads through soil by dark, cord-like rhizomorphs and can kill living trees as well as decay dead stumps. Other species, such as the tinder fungus, Fomes fomentarius, on beech and birch, begin as parasites on weakened hosts and continue to fruit long after the tree has died.

True saprotrophs arrive after death. The turkey tail, Trametes versicolor, and the many crust fungi that spread thinly over the underside of fallen branches belong to this group. Their fruiting bodies may be small and easily overlooked, yet they carry out much of the work of decay.

Succession and competition

Decomposition of a log is not the work of a single organism. Wood is colonised by a sequence of fungi, beginning with spores or latent fungal tissue already present within living sapwood, called endophytes. Early colonists are often replaced by stronger competitors, and the boundaries between rival individuals can be seen in cut wood as dark, narrow lines, sometimes called zone lines. These mark territories that adjacent fungal bodies defend chemically and physically against one another.

Ecological significance

Dead and decaying wood supports a large community. Beetle larvae feed on fungus-softened timber or on the fungi themselves, and fungus gnats, mites, slime moulds and mosses occupy the same habitat. Woodpeckers excavate softened trunks, and cavity-nesting birds and bats later use the holes, as do small mammals. Many of these relationships depend on the presence of old trees and large pieces of deadwood, which is why forests managed for tidiness often support fewer fungal and invertebrate species than those where fallen timber is left in place.

Through their work, wood-decay fungi release carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and pass mineral nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, back to the soil, where they become available to tree roots and mycorrhizal partners. Decay thus links the life of the canopy with the processes of the forest floor.

Mushrooms of the Forest Floor

The conspicuous mushrooms that appear on the floor of a temperate deciduous forest are only the reproductive structures of fungi whose main bodies lie hidden in soil, leaf litter and wood. This body, the mycelium, is a branching network of fine threads called hyphae. It absorbs nutrients from its surroundings and may persist for many years. The mushroom, or fruiting body, is produced when conditions allow, and its task is to shed spores. Because fruiting depends on moisture, temperature and the condition of the mycelium, the same patch of woodland may yield abundant mushrooms in one autumn and very few in the next.

Ecological roles

Forest fungi are usually grouped by how they obtain food. Three broad groups are important on the forest floor.

Saprotrophic fungi decompose dead organic matter. Some break down fallen leaves and needles, while others specialise in dead wood. Wood-decaying species differ in the enzymes they use. White rot fungi are able to degrade lignin, the tough compound that stiffens wood, and often leave the remaining wood pale and fibrous. Brown rot fungi mainly attack cellulose and leave a dark, crumbly residue. Through these activities fungi return carbon and mineral nutrients to the soil and make them available to other organisms.

Mycorrhizal fungi form partnerships with the roots of living trees. The fungus extends the effective reach of the root system, helping the tree to take up water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and in exchange receives sugars made by the tree through photosynthesis. Oaks, beeches, birches, hornbeams and many other deciduous trees depend on such associations, particularly the type known as ectomycorrhiza, in which the fungus forms a sheath around the root tips. Many familiar woodland mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of these partners.

Parasitic and pathogenic fungi attack living plants. Some, such as honey fungus, can kill trees weakened by other stresses, and they also live on dead wood. Their effect on a forest is not simply destructive, since the death of individual trees opens gaps in the canopy and creates habitat for other species.

Familiar groups

Several groups of mushrooms are characteristic of deciduous woodland. Boletes have a spongy layer of tubes rather than gills beneath the cap and are often associated with particular tree species. Russulas and milkcaps are brittle-fleshed mycorrhizal fungi; milkcaps exude a fluid when cut. Amanitas include some of the most recognisable woodland species, among them the fly agaric, which is often found with birch, and the death cap, which is associated mainly with oaks and other broadleaved trees and is responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings. Chanterelles and their relatives have blunt, gill-like ridges and grow in association with trees such as beech and oak. Bracket fungi form shelves on trunks and logs, and some, like the tinder fungus, persist for many seasons. Small decomposers, including species of Mycena, appear in great numbers on leaf litter and twigs. Earthstars, puffballs and stinkhorns release spores in different ways, from puffs of dust to a sticky, odorous slime that attracts insects.

Seasonal pattern

In temperate regions the main fruiting season is autumn, when falling temperatures and increased rainfall coincide with a thick supply of fresh leaf litter. Some species appear in spring, and others fruit in early summer after rain. Many bracket fungi can be found at any time of year. Mushrooms themselves are short-lived and are quickly eaten by slugs, insect larvae, small mammals and other animals, which also help to carry spores to new sites.

Identification and caution

Identifying mushrooms requires attention to several features, including cap, gills or pores, stem, ring or volva, spore print colour, habitat and associated trees. Because several poisonous species resemble edible ones, a mushroom should never be eaten on the basis of a casual resemblance. Collecting for food is best done with expert guidance, and local rules on gathering in protected woodland should be observed.

Parasitic and Pathogenic Fungi

Fungi that feed on living trees occupy an ambiguous place in temperate deciduous forests. Some kill their hosts rapidly and alter the composition of entire stands. Others persist for decades in a tree's heartwood or roots, weakening it slowly and shaping its later life. Many are opportunists that attack only trees already stressed by drought, frost, defoliation or injury. Because the boundary between parasite, pathogen and decomposer is often blurred, a single species may behave differently depending on the vigour of the host and the conditions of the site.

Root and butt pathogens

The honey fungi of the genus Armillaria are among the most widespread tree pathogens of northern forests. They spread through the soil as dark, bootlace-like rhizomorphs, which grow from infected stumps and roots and attach to the roots of nearby trees. Once beneath the bark, the fungus forms white mycelial fans that kill the cambium, and it then continues into the wood as a white rot. Individual colonies can occupy large areas of forest floor and persist for very long periods. Armillaria often acts as a secondary agent, killing trees weakened by other causes, but in some circumstances it attacks healthy trees. Its clusters of honey-coloured fruit bodies appear in autumn at the bases of infected trees and stumps.

Heterobasidion, the cause of annosum root rot, is better known as a conifer pathogen but also occurs on some broadleaved trees in mixed woods. It spreads by airborne spores that colonise fresh stumps and then passes through root contacts to neighbouring trees.

Heart rots and bracket fungi

Many bracket fungi enter living trees through wounds, broken branches or dead branch stubs and then decay the heartwood without immediately killing the tree. The tinder fungus Fomes fomentarius, common on beech and birch, and the sulphur polypore Laetiporus sulphureus, found on oak and other broadleaves, are typical examples. Species of Ganoderma and Phellinus similarly rot the base or trunk. A tree with a hollowed core can remain standing and productive for a long time, because the living sapwood continues to carry water and nutrients. The cavities that develop provide nesting and roosting sites for woodpeckers, owls, bats and many invertebrates, so the activity of these fungi supports a considerable part of the forest's animal life. Eventually the structural weakening leads to breakage or windthrow, which returns the wood to the decomposer community.

Vascular wilts and cankers

The most dramatic losses have been caused by pathogens moved between continents with plant material or timber. Dutch elm disease is caused by Ophiostoma ulmi and the later, far more aggressive Ophiostoma novo-ulmi. The fungi are carried by elm bark beetles, which introduce spores into the xylem when they feed in young twigs. The tree responds by blocking its own vessels, and this defence contributes to the wilting and death of the crown. Epidemics in Europe and North America removed most mature elms from many landscapes during the twentieth century.

Chestnut blight, caused by Cryphonectria parasitica, was introduced from East Asia to North America and recorded in New York in the early 1900s. It forms cankers that girdle stems. The American chestnut, once a dominant tree of eastern forests, was reduced largely to sprouts that grow from surviving root systems and are repeatedly killed back. Asian chestnut species evolved alongside the fungus and are far more resistant.

Ash dieback, caused by Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, arrived in Europe from East Asia and was first noticed in the 1990s. It spreads by wind-borne spores released from fruit bodies on fallen ash leaf stalks, and it causes leaf loss, crown death and bark lesions. Fungi that colonise weakened ash, including Armillaria, often hasten the decline.

Foliar and complex diseases

Powdery mildews, notably Erysiphe alphitoides on oak, and leaf-spot fungi such as the anthracnoses usually do limited harm to mature trees but can damage seedlings and young growth. Beech bark disease involves a sap-feeding scale insect and canker fungi of the genus Neonectria, which invade the bark through feeding wounds. Sudden oak death is caused by Phytophthora ramorum, which is an oomycete, a fungus-like organism not closely related to true fungi, though it is often discussed alongside them.

Ecological significance

Pathogens contribute to forest dynamics by opening gaps, promoting regeneration and creating standing and fallen deadwood. Introduced diseases, however, can remove a species faster than the forest can adapt, with lasting consequences for the animals and fungi that depend on it.

Slime Molds and Fungus-like Organisms

The floor of a temperate deciduous forest supports a group of organisms that were long classified with fungi but are now understood to belong to quite different lineages. Slime molds, water molds and their relatives resemble fungi in their habit of growing through decaying material and producing spores, yet they differ in cell structure, feeding method and evolutionary origin. Their ecological roles in leaf litter, rotting wood and soil are nonetheless similar to those of true fungi, and they are commonly encountered in the same places.

Plasmodial slime molds

The plasmodial slime molds, or myxomycetes, are among the most conspicuous of these organisms. During the feeding stage, the organism exists as a plasmodium, a single mass of protoplasm containing many nuclei and no internal cell walls. The plasmodium creeps over fallen logs, bark and damp leaf litter, engulfing bacteria, yeasts, fungal spores and fragments of organic matter. It often forms a branching network of veins through which cytoplasm streams in rhythmic pulses, and it can move toward food and away from light or dryness.

When conditions change, usually through drying or exhaustion of food, the plasmodium transforms into fruiting bodies that release spores. These structures vary widely in form. Some are small stalked spheres, others are tufts, nets or cushions, and many are colored yellow, orange, pink or white. Species of the genus Fuligo produce a spreading yellow mass on rotting wood and mulch. Lycogala forms small pinkish globes on decaying logs, and Stemonitis forms clusters of slender brown stalks. Fruiting is most often seen in autumn and after warm spells of rain, although some species appear in cold weather beneath snow cover or at the edge of melting snow.

Cellular slime molds

The cellular slime molds are a separate group. Their feeding stage consists of individual amoebae that live in soil and litter and consume bacteria. When food becomes scarce, the amoebae release chemical signals and aggregate into a multicellular slug that migrates before forming a small fruiting structure with a stalk and a spore mass. The species Dictyostelium discoideum has been studied extensively in the laboratory as a model of cell signaling and development, but its natural home is the soil of deciduous forests. Cellular slime molds are generally microscopic as individuals and are rarely noticed in the field.

Water molds and related oomycetes

Oomycetes, often called water molds, are filamentous organisms that were once grouped with fungi because of their threadlike growth. Their cell walls contain cellulose rather than chitin, and they are more closely related to brown algae and diatoms than to fungi. Many live in streams, pools and saturated forest soils, where they decompose dead insects and plant debris.

Some oomycetes are significant pathogens of trees. Species of Phytophthora cause root and collar rots and cankers in a range of forest trees. Phytophthora ramorum, responsible for sudden oak death, has affected oaks and other woody plants in parts of North America and Europe. The disease illustrates how organisms outside the true fungi can alter forest composition, particularly when introduced to regions where native trees have little resistance.

Ecological role

Slime molds contribute to nutrient cycling by feeding on bacteria and other microbes, which regulates microbial populations and releases nutrients bound in microbial tissue. Their fruiting bodies provide food and shelter for small beetles, fly larvae and other invertebrates. Because many species depend on moist, decaying wood and bark, they are most diverse in forests that retain fallen timber and a continuous layer of litter. Their presence is therefore sometimes taken as one indicator of the structural complexity of a woodland.

Resident Forest Birds

Resident birds are those that remain in a temperate deciduous forest throughout the year, in contrast to migrants that arrive to breed or pass through on their way to wintering grounds. Residents must cope with the full range of seasonal change, from the abundance of leaf-eating insects in late spring to the scarcity of food and the long, cold nights of winter. Their behaviour, anatomy and social organisation reflect this demand, and many of them play an important part in the movement of seeds, the control of insect populations and the creation of nesting sites used by other species.

Woodpeckers and Other Bark Foragers

Woodpeckers are among the most conspicuous residents. Species such as the great spotted woodpecker of Eurasia and the downy and hairy woodpeckers of eastern North America chisel into dead or decaying wood to reach beetle larvae and other insects. Stiff tail feathers act as a prop against the trunk, and the feet have two toes pointing forward and two back for gripping bark. In autumn and winter many species also take seeds and nuts, and some wedge them into crevices to be hammered open. Cavities excavated by woodpeckers are often reused in later years by owls, flycatchers, bats and small mammals, which makes the birds a keystone resource in mature woodland.

Nuthatches and treecreepers forage on the same trunks in different ways. Nuthatches descend head-first as well as climbing, inspecting crevices that upward-moving birds overlook. Treecreepers spiral upward from the base of one tree and then fly to the base of the next, probing bark with slender, curved bills.

Tits, Chickadees and Winter Flocks

The tits of Europe and the chickadees of North America are small, active insectivores that switch to seeds and stored food in the cold months. Many store food in bark crevices and other hiding places, and are thought to remember where it is cached. Outside the breeding season they often assemble into mixed-species flocks that may include nuthatches, treecreepers, small woodpeckers and kinglets. Flocking is generally understood to improve the detection of predators and to help individuals find scattered food, although the benefits vary between species and between flock members of different rank.

Corvids and Seed Dispersal

Jays, crows and their relatives are intelligent, adaptable residents. The Eurasian jay and the blue jay gather acorns and beechnuts in autumn and bury them in the soil or leaf litter. Because not every cache is recovered, these birds have acted as significant dispersers of oak and beech, and they may carry heavy seeds farther than mammals or gravity alone would. This relationship is one reason the spread of oaks after the retreat of the last glaciation is often discussed in connection with jays.

Owls and Raptors

Tawny owls, barred owls and similar species hold territories year-round, often nesting in natural tree hollows. They hunt small mammals, especially rodents, by sound and sight in low light. Sparrowhawks and goshawks, adapted with short, broad wings and long tails for manoeuvring among branches, prey on other birds and are a main cause of mortality among small woodland residents.

Ground and Understorey Species

Thrushes, wrens, robins and some game birds use the leaf litter and shrub layer. The European robin and the winter wren glean invertebrates from the forest floor, while wild turkeys and pheasants scratch for seeds, nuts and insects. Dense understorey vegetation provides cover for nests and shelter in winter.

Seasonal Rhythms

Residents begin to establish territories in late winter, when song increases and pairs form. Breeding is timed so that nestlings are fed during the brief peak in caterpillar numbers that follows leaf emergence. Warmer springs have in some regions shifted this peak earlier, and the match between bird breeding and food supply is an active subject of research. After breeding, territories break down, young birds disperse and the winter flocks reform.

Migratory Songbirds

Each spring, temperate deciduous forests in eastern North America, Europe and East Asia receive a seasonal influx of small insect-eating birds that breed in the woodland and spend the rest of the year far to the south. These migratory songbirds, often called Neotropical migrants in the New World and trans-Saharan migrants in Europe, are among the most conspicuous elements of the forest's seasonal life. Their arrival is closely tied to the leafing of the trees and the emergence of the insects that feed on new foliage.

Timing and Food

Migrants such as wood warblers, vireos, thrushes, tanagers and flycatchers time their northward movement to the flush of caterpillars and other invertebrates that appear as buds break. Many caterpillars feed on the tender young leaves of oaks, maples, birches and other canopy trees, and their abundance is brief. Nestlings are fed almost entirely on soft-bodied insects, so breeding that coincides with this peak gives young birds the best chance of survival. In the European pied flycatcher, for example, studies since the late twentieth century have shown that warmer springs can advance the caterpillar peak, leaving late-arriving birds out of step with their food supply. This mismatch is one of several concerns raised by climate change.

Birds use daylength and internal annual rhythms to prepare for departure, and most travel at night, resting and feeding in woodland patches by day. Stopover habitat is therefore important. Forest fragments along coasts and river valleys can hold large numbers of tired migrants after a night crossing of open water or desert.

Habitat Use Within the Forest

Different species occupy different layers of the forest, which reduces competition. Ovenbirds and some thrushes forage and nest on or near the leaf-littered ground. Understory species, such as certain warblers and the wood thrush, use shrubs and saplings. Scarlet tanagers, many vireos and numerous warblers feed high in the canopy, gleaning insects from leaves and twigs. Cavity nesters, including some flycatchers and redstarts, depend on dead trees and old woodpecker holes, which link their success to the presence of mature and decaying timber.

Songs and Territories

The dawn chorus of late spring is produced mainly by males establishing territories and attracting mates. Song defends a nesting area and advertises condition, while shorter calls are used to keep contact and to warn of predators. The dense foliage of a summer forest limits visibility, which may help explain why so many woodland species rely on distinctive songs rather than bright plumage for communication.

Threats and Conservation

Many long-distance migrants have declined in recent decades. Contributing factors include loss and fragmentation of breeding woodland, destruction of wintering habitat in the tropics, collisions with buildings and towers, predation by domestic cats, and changing seasonal conditions. Fragmentation can expose nests to higher rates of predation and to brood parasitism by cowbirds in North America. Large, continuous tracts of forest generally support the most successful breeding populations of area-sensitive species.

Conservation measures include protecting extensive woodland, retaining standing dead trees, managing deer populations that overbrowse the understory, and reducing artificial light during migration periods. Because these birds depend on habitats in several countries, effective protection requires coordination across breeding, stopover and wintering regions.

Ecological Role

Migratory songbirds consume large numbers of herbivorous insects and may moderate damage to trees during outbreaks. They also disperse some seeds when they eat fruit in late summer and autumn before departure. In autumn, the departure of these birds marks a seasonal turning point, as the forest shifts toward its leafless winter state and resident species such as chickadees, nuthatches and woodpeckers remain.

Woodpeckers and Cavity Nesters

Woodpeckers occupy a central place in the animal life of temperate deciduous forests. Their habit of excavating chambers in living and dead wood shapes the structure of the forest in ways that extend well beyond the birds themselves. Many other animals depend on the holes they create, and the presence or absence of woodpeckers can influence which species are able to breed in a given stand.

Excavators and Their Tools

Woodpeckers are adapted for repeated impact against wood. The skull is reinforced, the bill is straight and chisel-like, and the stiff tail feathers act as a prop against the trunk. The feet are typically arranged with two toes pointing forward and two back, allowing a firm grip on vertical bark. The tongue is long and often barbed or sticky, and it is used to draw insects from tunnels in wood. Different species use these tools in different ways. Large species such as the pileated woodpecker of North America and the black woodpecker of Europe and Asia cut deep, rectangular or oval excavations in search of carpenter ants and beetle larvae. Smaller species, such as the downy woodpecker and the lesser spotted woodpecker, work on slender branches and twigs, taking insects from bark and small stems.

Foraging and Diet

Diet varies with season and species. In spring and summer, most woodpeckers feed largely on insects, including wood-boring beetle larvae, ants and caterpillars. In autumn and winter, nuts, acorns and fruit become more important for some species. The red-bellied woodpecker and the acorn woodpecker store food, and the latter is well known for drilling large numbers of small holes in a tree to hold acorns. Sapsuckers drill rows of shallow wells in the bark and return to drink the sap and take insects attracted to it. These wells are also used by hummingbirds, warblers, bats and insects.

Drumming and Territory

In late winter and spring, woodpeckers drum rapidly on resonant dead limbs, trunks and sometimes artificial objects. Drumming is not feeding behaviour. It serves to advertise a territory and attract a mate, and each species has a characteristic rhythm and duration. In a leafless forest early in the year, the sound carries a long distance and is often the first sign that a woodpecker is present.

Cavities as a Shared Resource

Most woodpeckers excavate a new nest cavity each breeding season, often in wood softened by fungal decay. Heart rot fungi, which break down the inner wood of living trees, make excavation easier, and many species choose trees that are already infected. This links woodpeckers directly to the fungal communities of the forest, and a tree with a sound outer shell and a decayed core is often ideal.

Abandoned woodpecker holes are then used by secondary cavity nesters, which cannot excavate their own. These include chickadees and tits, nuthatches, bluebirds, flycatchers, wrens, starlings, owls and small ducks such as the wood duck and goldeneye. Mammals also use them, including squirrels, dormice, bats and martens. Some of these species, such as the nuthatch, adjust the entrance with mud to exclude competitors or predators. Because the supply of suitable cavities is often limited, competition for them can be intense, and the number of holes available may restrict local breeding populations more than food does.

Dead Wood and Forest Management

Woodpeckers depend on standing dead trees, called snags, and on old trees with decaying heartwood. Forests that are intensively managed, with trees harvested before they age and dead wood removed, tend to hold fewer cavity-nesting species. Retaining snags, leaving some old and damaged trees, and allowing natural decay are widely recommended conservation measures. Where such features are scarce, nest boxes can supplement natural cavities, though they do not replace the ecological functions of old and dying trees.

Woodpeckers are often regarded as indicators of forest condition. The presence of larger species, which need substantial trunks and large areas of suitable habitat, usually suggests a forest with well-developed structure and a continuing supply of dead and decaying wood.

Raptors and Owls

Birds of prey occupy the upper levels of the food web in temperate deciduous forests. They feed on small mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and large insects, and their presence reflects the abundance and diversity of the animals beneath them. Diurnal raptors and nocturnal owls hunt the same woodland, but they divide it by time of day, by prey type and by preferred hunting habitat.

Diurnal Raptors

The most characteristic woodland hawks belong to the genus Accipiter. In Europe the Eurasian sparrowhawk and the northern goshawk fill this role, and in eastern North America the sharp-shinned hawk, Cooper's hawk and northern goshawk do. These birds have short, rounded wings and long tails, a combination that allows rapid acceleration and sharp turns between trunks and branches. They hunt mainly by surprise, flying low along rides, edges and clearings, or watching from a concealed perch before a short pursuit. Smaller species take songbirds, while larger ones take pigeons, jays, squirrels and rabbits.

Buteos, such as the common buzzard in Europe and the red-shouldered and broad-winged hawks in North America, are broader-winged and more often associated with the mix of forest and open ground. They hunt from perches or in soaring flight, and they take voles, mice, frogs, snakes and earthworms. The red-shouldered hawk is closely tied to mature, moist bottomland forest. The broad-winged hawk breeds in extensive deciduous and mixed woodland and migrates long distances in large flocks, called kettles, that use rising thermal air.

Other diurnal species use the forest more selectively. The European honey buzzard specialises in the larvae and combs of wasps and bees, which it digs from nests in the ground. Small falcons, including the Eurasian hobby, often nest in old crow nests at the edge of woodland but hunt over open country.

Owls

Owls are adapted to hunting in low light. Their large, forward-facing eyes are highly sensitive, and their hearing is acute. In several species the facial disc funnels sound to ears that are set asymmetrically on the skull, which helps the bird locate prey by sound alone. The soft edges of the flight feathers reduce noise in flight, so the owl can hear its prey and the prey is less likely to hear the owl.

The tawny owl is the typical woodland owl of Europe. It is largely sedentary, holds a territory throughout the year, and nests in tree cavities or in the old nests of other birds. Its diet changes with the seasons and includes woodland mice and voles, birds, and earthworms. In North America the barred owl plays a comparable part, and its rhythmic call is a familiar sound in mature forest. The smaller eastern screech-owl uses natural cavities and nest boxes, and the great horned owl takes larger prey, including other raptors, from forest and edge habitats.

Owls regurgitate the indigestible fur, feathers and bones of their prey as compact pellets. Collected beneath roosts, these pellets give researchers a direct record of diet and of the small mammals living in the area.

Dependence on Old Trees

Many forest raptors depend on features that develop slowly. Large, mature trees provide stable platforms for the stick nests of hawks, and decay and woodpecker work create the cavities that owls need. Forests managed for the removal of old and dead trees may therefore lose nesting owls even when prey remains plentiful. Retaining veteran trees, standing deadwood and structural variety is generally regarded as important for these birds.

Seasonal Patterns

Leaf fall changes hunting conditions. In winter the open canopy improves visibility and lets hunters see more of the woodland floor, but prey is scarcer and some small birds have left. Many owls begin territorial calling in late winter and breed early, so that the young hatch when food becomes more abundant in spring. Hawks usually nest as the leaves emerge, and the foliage then helps to conceal the nest.

Historically, persecution and the use of persistent pesticides caused severe declines in several raptor populations in the twentieth century. Legal protection and the restriction of the most harmful chemicals have allowed many of these species to recover in much of their range.

Bird Song and the Dawn Chorus

In temperate deciduous forests, the period shortly before and after sunrise in spring and early summer is marked by a dense concentration of bird vocalisation known as the dawn chorus. Singing begins in the half-light, often well before the first direct sunlight reaches the canopy, and builds in intensity as light increases. It then declines gradually through the morning, although some species continue to sing intermittently throughout the day. The chorus is most pronounced during the breeding season, when territorial males are establishing boundaries and attracting mates, and it is strongly seasonal in character, being largely absent in the leafless months of winter.

Function of Song

Song in forest birds serves two principal purposes: the defence of a territory against other males of the same species, and the advertisement of a male to prospective mates. Songs are distinct from the shorter calls used to signal alarm, maintain contact between flock members, or beg for food. In many species, song is learned during a sensitive period in early life, with young males copying the songs of adult neighbours. As a result, local dialects can develop, and individual males may be recognised by their neighbours through small differences in the arrangement of phrases.

Why the Chorus Occurs at Dawn

Several explanations have been proposed for the concentration of singing at dawn, and they are not mutually exclusive. One suggestion is that low light makes foraging inefficient, so that birds can spend this period singing at little cost to feeding. Another is that the cool, still air of early morning allows sound to travel farther, because there is less turbulence and temperature-driven scattering than later in the day. A further idea is that dawn is the moment when territorial status is most usefully reaffirmed after a night of inactivity, and that females are fertile and receptive at this time. Observers have also noted that males that sing vigorously at dawn demonstrate good condition, since they have survived the night and retained enough energy reserves to sing.

Order of Singing

The chorus does not begin all at once. Species tend to start in a fairly consistent sequence, a pattern that has been recorded in many European and North American woodlands. Birds with relatively large eyes, such as thrushes and robins, often start earliest, which is generally interpreted as an adaptation to seeing in dim light. Species with smaller eyes, including many warblers and finches, typically join later. In European woods the robin, blackbird and song thrush are commonly among the first voices, while in eastern North American forests species such as the wood thrush, veery and ovenbird contribute to the early sounds. The order can shift with latitude, weather and the stage of the breeding season.

Acoustic Structure of the Forest

The structure of the forest affects how song is transmitted. Dense foliage absorbs and scatters high-frequency sound, so species living low in the vegetation often use lower-pitched, simpler notes that carry better through leaves and trunks. Birds singing from the upper canopy or from exposed perches may use higher or more elaborate phrases. Because many species sing simultaneously, there is evidence that they partition the acoustic space by using different frequencies and rhythms, which reduces masking of one another's songs. The leaf-out of trees in spring changes this acoustic environment, so that a forest sounds different before and after the canopy closes.

Human Influences

Noise from roads, aircraft and settlements can overlap with the frequencies used by forest birds and make song harder to detect. Studies in several regions have found that some species sing at higher pitch, louder, or at different times of day in noisy surroundings. Artificial light at night has also been associated with earlier singing in some urban and suburban populations. Because bird song is conspicuous and relatively easy to survey, it is widely used by ornithologists to monitor the presence and abundance of forest species, and long-term recordings of the dawn chorus provide a record of how woodland communities respond to environmental change.

Deer, Squirrels, and Small Mammals

Mammals shape temperate deciduous forests through what they eat, what they bury, and where they travel. Many of the most conspicuous species depend on the seasonal pulse of food that the trees provide, and their activity in turn influences which seedlings survive, how seeds are dispersed, and how nutrients move through the soil.

White-tailed deer and their relatives

In eastern North America the white-tailed deer is the dominant large herbivore of deciduous woodland. In Europe the roe deer and red deer fill comparable roles, and in parts of East Asia sika deer and related species do so. These animals are browsers and grazers of mixed habits. In spring and summer they eat the leaves of herbs, shrubs, and young trees. In autumn they turn to acorns, beechnuts, and other mast, and in winter they rely on twigs, buds, evergreen ferns, and the bark of saplings.

Where deer are abundant, their effects on the forest can be pronounced. Selective browsing removes the seedlings of palatable species such as oaks, maples, and many wildflowers, while leaving unpalatable plants, including some ferns, spicebush, and invasive shrubs, to spread. Over several decades this can produce a forest with an open understory and little regeneration of canopy trees. Historically, predators such as wolves and cougars limited deer numbers in many regions. Their removal during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, together with the reduction of hunting pressure near settled areas, allowed deer populations to increase in many places.

Squirrels, chipmunks, and the dispersal of seeds

Tree squirrels are closely tied to nut-bearing trees. The gray squirrel and the fox squirrel of North America, and the red squirrel of Eurasia, gather acorns, hickory nuts, walnuts, and beechnuts in autumn. Much of this harvest is placed in scattered caches, each buried separately in the leaf litter or shallow soil. Squirrels do not recover every cache, and the nuts that remain may germinate. In this way squirrels act as planters of oaks and hickories, often moving seeds some distance from the parent tree.

Chipmunks behave differently. The eastern chipmunk carries food in cheek pouches to underground burrows, where it keeps a larder for winter. It enters periods of torpor rather than true continuous hibernation, waking to feed on its stores. Flying squirrels, which are nocturnal, glide between trunks and nest in tree cavities. They eat nuts, fungi, insects, and occasionally eggs or nestlings.

Mast years and population cycles

Oaks and beeches do not produce seed at a steady rate. They tend to have heavy crops in some years and light crops in others, a pattern called masting. After a heavy crop, populations of mice, squirrels, and chipmunks often rise in the following season, and the added numbers of small rodents can affect other species. Predators such as owls, foxes, and hawks may do well, while ground-nesting birds can suffer when rodents are plentiful and turn to eggs. Rodent abundance has also been linked, in some regions, to the abundance of ticks that carry disease, because mice are important hosts for the young stages of these parasites.

Mice, voles, shrews, and bats

Beneath the canopy, smaller mammals occupy the litter and soil. White-footed mice and deer mice forage for seeds, insects, and fungi, and they climb readily. Voles feed on roots, bark, and herbaceous growth, sometimes girdling young trees beneath winter snow. Shrews and moles hunt invertebrates in the leaf litter and topsoil. Their tunnelling mixes organic matter into the mineral layers and aerates the ground.

Many small mammals eat the fruiting bodies of fungi, including truffle-like species that grow underground. These animals digest little of the spores, which pass through the gut intact and are deposited elsewhere. This is one route by which mycorrhizal fungi, which partner with tree roots, reach new sites.

Bats, which roost in hollow trees and under loose bark, are important predators of night-flying insects in summer. Many species either migrate or hibernate in caves during winter, leaving the forest largely free of bat activity in the coldest months.

Predators and Carnivores

Predators occupy every layer of a temperate deciduous forest, from the leaf litter to the upper canopy, and their composition differs between the forests of eastern North America, western and central Europe, and eastern Asia. Although large carnivores once ranged across all three regions, many of the most conspicuous species have been reduced or eliminated by hunting and habitat loss. Smaller predators, including insects, spiders, amphibians, birds and mustelids, continue to shape the structure of forest food webs.

Invertebrate predators

The most numerous predators are invertebrates. Ground beetles hunt at night among fallen leaves, taking springtails, caterpillars, slugs and earthworms. Centipedes patrol the soil surface and the spaces between rotting logs, while harvestmen and wolf spiders capture small prey without webs. Web-building spiders are abundant in the understory and canopy, and their silk intercepts large numbers of flying insects. Parasitoid wasps and flies, which lay eggs in or on other insects, form a further group of predatory animals; their larvae consume the host from within and are a major cause of mortality among leaf-feeding caterpillars. Because caterpillar outbreaks can defoliate oaks and other trees, these natural enemies have an indirect influence on tree growth and seed production.

Amphibians and reptiles

Salamanders are important predators in the moist litter of eastern North American forests, where in some places they are among the most abundant vertebrates. They feed on mites, small insects and other invertebrates, and in doing so affect the rate at which litter is broken down. Frogs and toads use similar habitats in spring and summer, often moving to ponds or temporary pools to breed. Snakes such as rat snakes, garter snakes and, in Europe, the grass snake and smooth snake, feed on amphibians, nestlings, eggs and small mammals. In cooler regions many reptiles and amphibians spend the winter underground or beneath logs.

Birds of prey

Forest raptors are adapted to hunting among trunks and branches. Accipiters, such as the sparrowhawk and goshawk in Europe and the Cooper's hawk in North America, have short, rounded wings and long tails that allow rapid turns, and they ambush songbirds and small mammals. Broad-winged buteos, including the red-shouldered hawk and the common buzzard, hunt from perches and take rodents, amphibians and large insects. Owls are the main nocturnal bird predators. The tawny owl, barred owl and great horned owl nest in tree cavities, old stick nests or dense foliage, and many of them depend on mature trees that provide suitable sites. Owl pellets, the compacted undigested remains of prey, give researchers a record of local small mammal populations.

Mammalian carnivores

Small and medium-sized mammals fill many predatory roles. Shrews and moles feed on soil invertebrates, and shrews must eat frequently throughout the year. Weasels, stoats and martens hunt rodents, birds and eggs; the pine marten and the American marten use hollow trees and dense cover. Foxes, raccoons, badgers and skunks are opportunistic and take a mixed diet of small animals, insects, fruit and carrion. Bobcats and lynx are the principal wild cats of the forest, hunting hares, rabbits and deer fawns.

The largest predators include wolves, brown bears and black bears, along with the leopard and tiger in parts of eastern Asia. Bears are omnivorous, eating large quantities of acorns, nuts, berries and roots, and also insects and carrion. Wolves and, formerly, other large carnivores limited the numbers of deer and wild boar. Where they have been removed, browsing by deer can suppress the regeneration of tree seedlings and alter the composition of the understory. In several regions the return or reintroduction of wolves and other predators has prompted study of whether such effects spread through the food web, although the results vary with local conditions and the history of human land use.

Seasonal patterns

Predator activity follows the seasons. In spring, migratory birds arrive as insect numbers rise, and nest predation becomes most intense. In autumn, abundant seed crops support rodent populations, which in turn influence owls and small carnivores in the following year. In winter, snow cover makes some prey easier to track, while hibernating animals such as bears and many small mammals reduce their activity or retire to dens.

Bats and Nocturnal Life

When daylight fades in a temperate deciduous forest, the community changes character. Many of the birds that fill the canopy with song fall silent, and a different set of animals becomes active: bats, owls, moths, nocturnal beetles, small mammals, and amphibians. The night shift is less conspicuous than the day, but it carries out much of the forest's predation, pollination, and nutrient cycling.

Bats as Forest Predators

Bats are the only mammals capable of sustained flight, and in temperate woodland they are almost entirely insectivorous. Species differ in wing shape and echolocation, and these traits sort them into distinct foraging niches within the same stand of trees. Species with short, broad wings and quiet, high-frequency calls are agile fliers able to hunt close to foliage, and some can pick insects directly from leaves or bark. Species with long, narrow wings are faster and more efficient in open air, and they hunt above the canopy, along rides, or over clearings and water. Edge habitats, such as the margin between forest and meadow or the corridor of a stream, are often the most productive feeding areas because insects concentrate there.

Diet reflects what is available. Moths, beetles, flies, and caddisflies are all taken, and some bats specialise strongly in particular groups. Moths have evolved defences in response, including ears tuned to bat calls, and some species respond to an approaching bat by folding their wings and dropping. By consuming large quantities of insects, including species that feed on leaves, bats are thought to contribute to limiting herbivory in the canopy, although the size of this effect varies between forests and years.

Roosts and Old Trees

Bats depend on trees for shelter as much as for food. In summer, females gather in maternity colonies, where they bear and rear young, usually a single pup per year. Roosts are found in woodpecker holes, rot cavities, cracks left by lightning or frost, and spaces behind loose bark. Different species prefer different conditions, and many switch between several roosts over a season, so a colony requires a cluster of suitable trees rather than a single one. Old, large, and dead standing trees therefore have particular value, and forests managed for rapid timber turnover often lack the cavities that bats need. Woodpeckers play an indirect role, since the holes they excavate are later used by bats, nuthatches, and other animals.

Seasonal Rhythms and Hibernation
